prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Robins in the cottonwoods, holding still as the thin snow comes. The sun seems to flood them with blood. They have settled in the empty branches while the storm-lamps spit in your limbs, red evening swinging across the sky then dropping, ragged, into your frame to stay with you as you move and smile and have opinions. Then a woman’s torso white with dawn— their rich perch is yours, there is nothing you need to expect or retrieve, like warm fields floating toward an invisible moon. A person learns stone-throated composures and barters for days of calm weather, like a man in a dream who understands the answering pressure of eyes—you ask too much. But the birds are not reckless. Every minute their fat shapes are filling with sun, and I apprentice myself to their candor. Their bodies drift on the moving branches, solid— they are not taking and keeping. They are not torn papers in a rumor of wind, their small backs brown fields holding thunderclouds up. Inside their bodies, nothing falls to the earth and dies.

# Stillness in the Cottonwoods

As thin snow drifts through the cold air, robins settle motionless into the branches of the cottonwood trees. The setting sun catches them at just the right angle, and its light seems to flood their small bodies with a blood-red glow, transforming these ordinary birds into something luminous and startling. They do not stir; they simply rest, saturated with the color of the dying day.

From this vivid scene, the imagery begins to shift and turn inward. The red evening light does not remain external—it lodges within the speaker's own body, becoming part of him. This intensity then transforms again, gliding into the image of a woman's torso illuminated by dawn. In this movement, the boundaries between self and scene dissolve, suggesting an intimate merging in which the observer and the observed, the landscape and the beloved, become inseparably intertwined.

Against this backdrop of natural repose, the speaker sets the restless effort of human life. He reflects on all the striving that consumes us: the labor of learning composure, the constant bargaining we do in hopes of securing a moment's calm, the way we perpetually ask too much of ourselves and of the world. This human burden stands in sharp contrast to the birds, whose stillness requires no such struggle—it is simply their nature, unburdened and complete.

Importantly, the birds are not portrayed as careless or reckless in their ease. Rather, they are candid and grounded, honest in their being. They fill quietly with the last of the sunlight and drift solidly upon the branches, present and settled. There is no grasping in them, no clinging, no anxious reaching for what they do not have. Their tranquility comes not from indifference but from a deep and rooted wholeness.

In its final turn, the poem arrives at a vision of integrity embodied by these motionless birds—a state in which, as the poem puts it, "nothing falls to the earth and dies." The robins become a model of the completeness the speaker himself longs to attain: a way of being so whole and so at peace that nothing is lost, nothing is wasted, and nothing perishes for want of care. In their silent, blood-lit stillness, they hold out the promise of an integrity that the striving human heart can only aspire to reach.
outputs.L4:
# Apprentice to the Robins

The robins came in the pale hour before the snow began, settling into the bare arms of the cottonwoods as if the branches had been waiting all winter to receive them. I watched from the window as the first flakes drifted down—not the heavy, burdening snow of deep winter, but a light, hesitant falling, the kind that seems undecided about whether to arrive at all.

The sun, low and dying at the edge of the sky, spilled its light across the snow and stained it the color of blood. There was something almost violent in that beauty, as though the day itself were wounded, bleeding out its last warmth into the cold. And I felt, watching it, the old familiar turbulence rise in me—that human restlessness, the churning need to *become*, to reach beyond the present moment toward some imagined completion that always recedes as I approach it. My heart is a fist that will not open. My mind is a road that leads only to further roads.

But the robins did not strive.

They sat in the falling snow with a composure I have never known, their breasts the same red as the bleeding light, and they asked nothing of the afternoon. They did not lament the coming cold. They did not rage against the dying of the sun. They simply were—present, rooted, unafraid—as if existence itself were sufficient, as if to be a robin in a cottonwood in the first snow were the whole and perfect purpose of a life.

How is it that these small creatures have learned what I cannot? How is it that they carry within their feathered bodies a peace that I have chased across the length of my restless years and never once held in my hands?

And so I make this quiet vow: I will apprentice myself to the robins. I will study their candor—the way they meet the world without pretense or complaint. I will learn their steadfastness, the manner in which they hold their branches while the snow comes down and the light goes red and the day surrenders to the dark. I will unlearn my hunger to be elsewhere, my conviction that the here and now is merely a threshold to be crossed.

For in their unforced, grounded existence, I begin to glimpse another way of being—a life of acceptance rather than striving, of presence rather than pursuit. In the world the robins inhabit, nothing is wasted. Nothing is squandered on regret or longing. Everything belongs, and everything is held, and in that holding there is a strange and gentle mercy where nothing falls to the earth and dies.
outputs.L5:
# The Return of the Robins

The robins are among the most beloved birds in many parts of the world. They are easily recognized by their bright reddish-orange breasts and cheerful songs that fill gardens and woodlands, especially in the early morning hours.

Robins hold a special place in people's hearts, and they are often seen as a sign of changing seasons. In many regions, when the robins appear, they signal that spring is on its way. Their arrival brings a sense of renewal and hope after the long, cold winter months.

They are remarkably adaptable creatures. Robins can thrive in a variety of environments, from quiet forests to busy city parks. They build their nests in trees, shrubs, and sometimes even in unexpected places like garden sheds or window ledges. The care they show toward their young is admirable, as both parents work together to feed and protect their chicks.

When it comes to food, robins have a diverse diet. They enjoy eating worms, insects, berries, and seeds. It is common to see them hopping across lawns, pausing to listen, and then quickly pulling an earthworm from the soil. This behavior makes them fascinating to watch for bird lovers of all ages.

The robins also play an important role in nature. They help control insect populations and spread seeds through the berries they consume. In this way, they contribute to the health and balance of their ecosystems.

In conclusion, robins are wonderful birds that bring joy to those who observe them. They remind us of the beauty of nature and the changing rhythms of the seasons. Whether in the countryside or the city, the robins continue to capture our attention and warm our hearts.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem about robins perched in bare cottonwood trees during a light snowfall, using surreal imagery and comparing the birds' stillness to a kind of spiritual composure the speaker wants to learn.
counterfactuals.output:
# Congregation

The robins have arranged themselves like punctuation in a sentence the winter forgot to finish. Snow falls the way sleep falls on a child mid-question, and the cottonwoods hold up their thousand empty hands, palms open, having given away every leaf as if leaves were a currency that meant nothing here.

I count seven birds, then nine, then lose the number in the branches. Each one wears its red breast like a small door left ajar, and behind that door, I imagine, a room where nothing needs to happen. They do not shiver. They do not rehearse their leaving. The snow settles on their shoulders like the touch of someone who has decided, finally, to forgive you, and they receive it the way stones receive rain—without gratitude, without complaint, simply the fact of being touched.

How do they do it? I have spent my life leaning forward, a runner at the gun that never fires. But these birds have folded time into their feathers. They sit inside the falling as though falling were a kind of arriving. As though the cold were just another word for held.

I want to learn this. I want to be the still thing at the center of the weather, the dark note that does not resolve because it does not need to. The trees say nothing. The snow keeps its long white promise. And the robins, those small monks of the ordinary, close their eyes as if the whole gray sky were a bell they had already stopped ringing—as if silence, at last, were something you could wear.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a contemplative poem in the style of a modern free-verse poet, meditating on birds in winter and how they embody a way of being that humans, full of anxiety and expectation, struggle to achieve.
counterfactuals.output:
The Wintering

Look how they endure it—
the sparrows in the hedge,
the juncos working the frozen ground
for whatever the season allots them.

They do not rehearse the cold.
They do not lie awake
inside the long arithmetic of night,
subtracting what they had
from what remains.

I have spent my life
leaning into the next hour
like a man walking against wind,
certain that arrival
would finally unclench me.

But the chickadee
spends nothing on tomorrow.
It hangs upside down from the seedhead,
that small acrobat of the actual,
weighing exactly as much
as this moment asks it to.

What would it take
to be so unhoused of worry—
to meet the bare branch
and the bare sky
and call them, without flinching,
enough?

The birds are not brave.
Bravery is a human weather,
a thing we summon
against the storm we imagine.
They simply are
where they are,
feathered and undefended,
their hearts drumming
that impossible warmth
into the middle of January.

I stand at the window
holding my cup of heat,
my catalog of dreads,
my hope like a coat
I keep meaning to grow into—

and they teach me nothing,
because teaching would require
that they intend me.

They only go on
being wholly themselves
in the killing cold,
which is, perhaps,
the single sermon
I was never quiet enough
to hear.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a lyrical, image-rich passage that blends nature observation with abstract, dreamlike metaphors—robins, snow, blood-red sunset, a woman's torso at dawn—ending on a note about the birds holding something up inside themselves that never falls and dies.
counterfactuals.output:
The Robins Hold What Never Falls

Dawn comes like a woman turning in her sleep—the pale
curve of her torso rising from the blue dark, shoulders
of mist, a slow breath moving through the birches.

And the snow remembers nothing. It lies where it was told
to lie, a white page pressed against the throat of the field,
waiting for the first small print of feet.

Robins arrive the way old griefs arrive—suddenly,
already familiar, their breasts the color of a sunset
someone bled into the horizon and forgot to wipe away.

They are stitched from ember and from ash. They carry
the last red hour of yesterday tucked beneath their wings,
and when they open their throats the morning cracks
like a struck bell, spilling its clear water everywhere.

I have watched the sun go down like a wound that will not
close, blood-red and patient, staining the drifts
until the whole world seemed a bandage soaking through—

and still the birds sang. Still they turned their small
faces to the cold. What is it they know that we forget
between one winter and the next?

There is something they hold up inside themselves,
a lit thing, round and warm as a swallowed coal,
that the snow cannot reach and the dark cannot drink,
that the long night leans against and cannot topple—

something that does not fall, that does not die,
that they carry singing into every ruined dawn.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write me a poem about apprenticing myself to the candor of birds.
counterfactuals.output:
**Apprenticed to the Candor of Birds**

I came to them as students come,
empty-handed, asking to be taught
the grammar of the unguarded throat,
the way a sparrow spends itself
completely on the morning,
holding nothing back for later.

No bird has ever hedged a song.
The wren does not rehearse
a softer version of its need,
does not apologize for wanting,
for the raw insistence of its hunger
flung against the widening light.

I have been careful all my life,
folding my truths in tissue,
speaking sideways, saving face—
but the thrush knows only forward,
only the clean arithmetic
of saying exactly what it is.

So teach me, then, this fearless craft:
to name the thing and mean it,
to open my mouth on the branch of the day
and let whatever's true come out—
unhemmed, unhidden, whole—
the way a blackbird pays its debt to dawn

by simply, wildly singing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: I want a dense, surreal prose-poem about watching robins in a snowstorm that explores themes of stillness versus grasping, calm versus reckless wanting, using vivid and unexpected images throughout.
counterfactuals.output:
# Robins in the White Machinery

The robins arrive like small red arguments against the snow, and I am watching them from behind glass that fogs with my own wanting. Each bird a struck match held to the throat of winter. Each bird refusing to catch.

The snow does not want. This is its terrible genius. It falls the way forgiveness falls—without aim, without the clenched fist of intention—and covers the fence posts in their sleep, dresses the dead garden in a bride's indifference. I press my palm to the cold pane and feel how the glass wants nothing back from me, how it simply *is* the boundary, patient as a monk who has swallowed his own name.

But the robins. Oh, the robins are all appetite and tremor. They stab at the frozen ground like tiny prosecutors demanding testimony from the worms, from the seeds, from anything that might rise. They are the color of my hunger exactly—that arterial insistence, that *give me, give me* pulsing beneath the feathers. I love them because they are foolish. I love them because they have not learned what the snow knows: that to fall softly is to arrive everywhere at once.

I have spent my life like a robin. Beak-first into the concrete of my own desires. Chest puffed red with the fever of *more.* And what did I catch? A handful of frost. A season's worth of scratching at a surface that would not open.

The storm thickens now into a white forgetting. The robins blur, become rumors of themselves, punctuation dissolving mid-sentence. And still they hunt, these little engines of yes, these feathered contradictions to the falling calm. One tilts its head. Listens to the earth the way a safecracker listens. Then drives its face into the cold again, gambling everything on the possibility of a single squirming reward.

I want to tell them: *Be the snow.* Let go of the grasping. Dissolve your red urgency into the great indifferent drift, and you will possess the whole white field by wanting none of it.

But I am lying. I am always lying when I preach surrender.

Because I love them more than I love the snow. Because the snow will never know it is beautiful, will never suffer, will never risk its soft anonymous body against the frozen mouth of the world. The robins *risk.* The robins burn. The robins are the only warm thing in the whole reckless afternoon, and they are warm precisely because they refuse to be still, because they want with their entire quaking bodies, because they have not made peace and will not make peace and would rather starve mid-flight than settle into the wise cold silence I keep almost, almost achieving.

The glass fogs again with my breath.

Somewhere beneath the white machinery, a worm turns in its dark bed, dreaming it is safe.

It is not safe.

Nothing that lives is ever safe, and this—*this*—is the only prayer the robins know.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
